item.title: Humor as a Psychological Defense Mechanism
item.description:
Defense Mechanisms

Humor as a Psychological Defense Mechanism

A laugh eases stress, but class clowns may be defending against emotional pain.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Laughter releases endorphins and is correlated to improvements in physical pain, depression, and anxiety.
  • Humor can also be a psychological defense, from easing social tension to shielding emotional turmoil.
  • If humor is disruptive, exploring the need for constant joking may help identify and resolve emotional pain.
Source: RDNE Stock Project / Pexels

They say that laughter is the best medicine. If you’ve ever been having a hard day but then told a good joke or, better yet, caught off guard by something comedic, you can likely attest to how levity can break the spell of gloom.

Interestingly, even nonhumorous laughter, like in laughter yoga, has been correlated to reduced pain, depression, anxiety, stress, and sleep problems (e.g., Uner et al., 2022). This is because laughter, whether humorous or not, triggers the release of endorphins, or “feel-good chemicals,” which not only boost mood but also contribute to relaxation of muscles (e.g., Hajar, 2023). Even better, an increase in endorphins decreases stress hormones, which can be damaging to our immune system (e.g., Alotiby, 2024), and regular laughter has been correlated with improvement in physical ailments (e.g., Oliveira & Arriaga, 2022; Singh et al., 2025).

Aside from the above, humor is also health-related in its role as a psychological defense mechanism.

Psychological defenses

These are subconscious cognitive processes that serve to protect against things that would be too anxiety-provoking to consciously acknowledge, guard against low self-esteem, and loss of self-integration (Cramer, 2008). While the term “defense” can have a negative or pejorative connotation (e.g., “S/he is so defensive!”), everyone has psychological defenses, which begin in childhood as adaptive responses to the world/people around the child. They develop at the intersection of temperament, the nature of stresses suffered early on, defenses modeled by important figures, and the reinforcement effects of using the defense(s) (McWilliams, 2011).

One common defense is withdrawal. On the healthy, “everyday” end of the spectrum, some people retreat into fantasy daydreaming when under stress. On the pathological side, withdrawal can be the foundation for personality disturbance. Personality is one’s way of relating to themselves, others, and the world around them. People who are temperamentally overstimulated and perhaps grew up in an environment with an emotionally cold and intrusive mother (McWilliams in Feinstein, 2022) may retreat more permanently into withdrawal as they age, shaping their general personality. Remaining detached from others ensures stimulation control and that they won’t be engulfed or intruded upon. This is prototypical of the schizoid personality, schizoid meaning there is a schism between their interpersonal behavior and the person’s inner experience. Schizoid people actually fantasize about having healthy relationships, but the fear of vulnerability is too great.

How humor works as a psychological defense

Humor, on the other hand, may be more familiar as a defense than many realize. This doesn’t mean that people with a sharp sense of humor are defensive. Like most things, it depends on the circumstance and the person. Who hasn’t encountered someone that is quick to make light of an awkward situation to ease the tension? Imagine a disagreeable colleague criticizing everyone and storming out of a meeting. Everyone looks around at each other uncomfortably for a minute, then someone says, “You don’t see that every day.” Some chuckles erupt, and the meeting continues. Humor can also help ease socio-political tension and draw people together, something prevalent in stand-up comedy. After 9/11, for example, Robin Williams in his “Live on Broadway” performance joked about how even the toughest New Yorkers were being nice to each other, a comedic reminder of the importance of unity and neighborly support in the face of the national tragedy.

Source: Cottonbro / Pexels

On the other hand, there are people who chronically use humor, which can be a double-edged sword, like the people I experience who come to rely heavily on withdrawal. Consider children who are disruptive class clowns. The kids I evaluate who exhibit this characteristic oftentimes have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). They can be very restless, struggle to keep still and pay attention, and thus feel marginalized alongside their classmates. They might expel that energy by doing silly things that will get some laughs, boosting their esteem, but nonetheless find themselves in the principal’s office for being too disruptive on other days, lowering their self- image.

Still others’ use of it as a defense is more sophisticated and has payoffs beyond shielding themselves from emotional pain. Many comedians have shared that it was their difficult childhood experiences that led to their successful comedy career. The late comedian Chris Farley, for example, was picked on for being an overweight child (Frommer, n.d.). He figured out that if he made jokes about his weight (imagine the “fat guy in a little coat” scene from Tommy Boy playing out in middle school), others were less likely to do so, and he gained popularity as a funny guy. This preemptive strike humor helped him deal with early bullying and led to his career success. Unfortunately, he self-medicated whatever pain the humor didn’t relieve, and died from an accidental overdose. Nevertheless, his penchant for humor made his life more bearable.

Rethinking the class clown

The next time you encounter someone who can’t seem to take anything seriously or is the rambunctious class clown, think of the paired tragedy and comedy masks of ancient Greek theater, representing the duality of human experience. They just might be protecting themselves from something painful and need someone to take them seriously and help them through what’s going on behind the clown façade. It could be as easy as a probation officer or school counselor asking a kid, “I know you like to make people laugh, but sometimes it seems like you can't stop being silly, and it gets you in trouble. What’s going on inside or in the classroom when you start to feel like clowning around?”

In the meantime, tell some jokes or find some laughter yoga. Your body and mind will thank you for it!

Disclaimer: The material provided in this post is for informational purposes only and is not intended to diagnose, treat, or prevent any illness in readers or people they know. The information should not replace personalized care or intervention from an individual’s provider or formal supervision if you’re a practitioner or student.

item.title: Why Myths Still Matter: Did Odysseus Suffer From PTSD?
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

Why Myths Still Matter: Did Odysseus Suffer From PTSD?

What ancient myths can teach us about psychopathology and psychotherapy today.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Posttraumatic stress disorder is not a new phenomenon.
  • Sudden exposure to existential evil is a key cause of PTSD.
  • Consciously facing and coming to terms with rather than avoiding one's inner demons is the key to recovery.

In Part 2 of this series on myths, I proposed that the heroic protagonist Odysseus, portrayed by actor Matt Damon in their new film "The Odyssey" (2026), directed by Christopher Nolan, intentionally or not, appears to suffer from what we would today diagnose as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Here in Part 3, we dive a little deeper into the psychology of PTSD and how psychotherapy can help in the process of healing it.

Antikes Relief, das die Sage von Odysseus und Polyphem darzustellen scheint.
Source: Jean-Pierre Houël, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Encountering the Existential Reality of Evil

The phenomenon of what we today call PTSD is not new. It has likely existed throughout human history. What causes it? Sudden or unexpected exposure to the existential reality of evil. (See my prior post.) By "evil," I am referring here to "man's inhumanity to man," (i.e., human evil such as violence, hatred, cruelty, sadism, misogyny, antisemitism, genocide, racism, etc.) as well as to terrifying catastrophic natural events or so-called "acts of god" like earthquakes, floods, famine, and tornadoes, as well as the inescapable facts of disease, and death (i.e., natural evil). Unanticipated exposure to evil or destructiveness in others or in nature—and, sometimes, in ourselves, as for instance, when we act out our "shadow"—traumatizes human beings, both on an individual and collective level.

Because we tend to deny its reality, most of us are not psychologically, emotionally, philosophically, or spiritually prepared for the experience of evil and, therefore, find it difficult to accept, process, and make sense of. It often does not comport with or contradicts our view of the world, others, or ourselves. It challenges, undermines, and sometimes shatters or destroys our sense of safety and security and erodes our ability to trust others, ourselves, and existence in general. It engenders painful losses: friends, family, home, material belongings, health, finances, employment, and, perhaps most importantly, the loss of meaning. Indeed, the abrupt confrontation with evil can cause us to question the meaning of life and leave us in a state of meaninglessness, nihilism, and despair. This is why patients diagnosed with PTSD commonly also suffer (like Odysseus apparently) from both depression and anxiety caused by their loss of faith in people (and perhaps in god or the gods), life, and goodness, as well as tormenting feelings of existential guilt about their own participation in evil, and a profound sense of existential insecurity and fear of the future. We see many of these symptoms and reactions in Nolan and Damon's somewhat tepid characterization of Odysseus.

By definition, PTSD can be the consequence of unwanted and unanticipated direct or indirect exposure to "actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence" (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition, Text Revision). Not everyone who has such traumatic experiences necessarily develops or meets full diagnostic criteria for a mental disorder per se, due, presumably, to individual differences in temperament, psychological history, religiosity or spirituality, resilience, support system, etc., but no one is totally immune to the trauma of evil. Military personnel are particularly prone to PTSD because they are more likely to be exposed to the horrors and atrocities of war. This was the case with Odysseus, who had survived a decade of hand-to-hand fighting during the Trojan War and ultimately participated in the savage sacking of the city of Troy. During the course of the film, we see him having what look like "flashbacks" (i.e., reexperiencing in the present the traumas of the past), a classic PTSD symptom consisting in his case of not only brutally killing enemy soldiers but also slaughtering innocent women and children. Odysseus appears to have been profoundly traumatized by the evil deeds he both witnessed and perpetrated during the prolonged campaign against Troy.

Suffering From Reminiscences

Fundamentally, what this most recent movie version of "The Odyssey" emphasizes psychologically is the perennial and traumatizing problem of evil and our all-too-human tendency toward unconsciousness: ignoring, forgetting, or denying the painful or anxiety-provoking past, present, and future. As Freud and Breuer (1895) observed, neurotic patients (and we are all neurotic) "suffer mainly from reminiscences." Such is the case with PTSD. For Odysseus, the wish to forget his horrific memories and painful feelings of guilt and regret about the past—missing his wife and son, his and his fellow soldiers' atrocities during the destruction of Troy (including their unethical sneak attack with the Trojan Horse, which, according to Odysseus himself, violated the "law of Zeus"), the violent and horrifying loss of friends and comrades both in battle and on the subsequent disastrous decade-long voyage home—evidently proves too much for Odysseus to deal with, turning him into a lost, homeless, disoriented, dissociated, "shell-shocked" wanderer who isn't psychologically ready to return to and deal with reality. This is a theme that was also explored exceptionally well in Nolan's far more interesting films "Memento" (2000) and "Inception" (2010).

The Long, Bumpy, and Labyrinthine Way Home

The trauma of evil is not limited to PTSD but is an inevitable and inescapable part of the human condition. It is merely a matter of degree and duration. We frequently see this phenomenon today in psychotherapy, whether in those experiencing PTSD symptoms or suffering from other debilitating psychiatric conditions such as panic disorder, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, psychotic disorders, and substance use disorders. These traumatized patients, much like the damaged Odysseus we meet in Nolan's film, choose unconsciousness, oblivion, fantasy, denial, distraction, dissociation, or ignorance over reality. Their own tragic odyssey is typically similar to that of Odysseus: an ill-fated flight from their torturous memories by whatever means necessary. But if they can summon up the heroic courage (like Odysseus sailing into Hades or hell) to enter and commit to psychotherapy and, like Odysseus or Hercules (see my prior post), to persevere, survive, do battle with, and surmount the many monstrous metaphorical demons, obstacles, and crises placed in their path by life, fate, or the gods, their own therapeutic and spiritual odyssey can eventually take them home to themselves and the life they truly want to live.

For Odysseus, the crucial final phase of this journey toward home is marked by him relinquishing control and allowing his ego to surrender to and trust the winds and currents of the sea (the unconscious), which eventually take him back to Ithaca. To paraphrase C.G. Jung on the subject of wholeness and the perilous voyage toward becoming oneself, the long, bumpy, and labyrinthine road (or longissima via) to individuation is fraught with fateful detours, dead-ends, wrong turns, potholes, flat tires, mechanical breakdowns, etc. But if we can bravely persist on this arduous journey, following our own instincts, intuition, inner GPS, or Ariadnean thread, we will, like Odysseus, eventually arrive at our destination.

item.title: Please Stop Calling Everyone a Narcissist
item.description:
Narcissism

Please Stop Calling Everyone a Narcissist

Describing harmful behavior is more useful than assigning a diagnosis.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Someone can have narcissistic traits without having narcissistic personality disorder.
  • “Narcissist” has become shorthand for almost any difficult, selfish, or hurtful person.
  • Labels can make it harder to identify and talk about the behavior that is actually causing the problem.

Not long ago, I wrote about my frustration with the way we use the word trigger. I hear another word being thrown around just as casually, and maybe even more often—narcissist. “My ex is a narcissist.” “My mother is a narcissist.” “He only cares about himself. Total narcissist.” Maybe...but probably not because of the reasons given.

Somewhere along the way, narcissist became our catch-all word for people who are selfish, controlling, arrogant, emotionally immature, difficult, manipulative, or just really bad partners. Those behaviors can absolutely be harmful and can make relationships miserable. They can be reasons to set boundaries, limit contact with a family member, find another job, or even end a relationship. But none of them, on their own, make someone a narcissist.

A Trait Is Not a Diagnosis

Narcissism isn’t an all-or-nothing characteristic. People can have narcissistic traits. In fact, most of us have moments where we act the way a narcissist might. Someone can enjoy being the center of attention. Someone can be overly concerned with status, or have a hard time ever admitting they’re wrong. Someone can be entitled, defensive, vain, insensitive, maddeningly self-absorbed…any one of a number of unpleasant things to be. That doesn’t automatically mean that person has narcissistic personality disorder (NPD).

NPD is an actual mental health diagnosis. Like other personality disorders, it involves an enduring pattern that extends across situations and significantly affects a person’s life and relationships. Diagnosing it requires more than hearing one person’s description of an ugly breakup. Yet, I regularly hear people confidently diagnosing partners, parents, friends, coworkers, and exes they are angry with. Often the person using the label isn’t a mental health professional. And even when they are, clinicians don’t diagnose people they’ve never evaluated. TikTok certainly can’t do it for you!

The Label Can Become a Shortcut

When someone says, “My husband is a narcissist,” I still don’t know what happened. Did he dismiss your feelings? Make major decisions without considering you? Criticize you and then tell you you’re too sensitive when you get upset? Does he expect you to accommodate his needs while rarely accommodating yours, or refuse to take responsibility when he hurts you? Those things tell me something. Just saying the word “narcissist” doesn’t. This is the same problem I have with the casual use of "triggered." We reach for a psychological term and, ironically, become less psychologically precise. In these situations, the label replaces the description.

Honestly, I understand that it is just easier to say. It takes less out of you to announce, “He’s a narcissist,” than it does to say, “When I tell my partner I’m hurt, he turns the conversation around until I’m the one apologizing.” That second sentence requires you to be specific and a little exposed. It may even invite a follow-up question you don’t have a prepared answer to. The label asks almost nothing of you, which is part of why it’s so tempting to use.

But the description is the one that actually gives us something to work with. It identifies a pattern and tells us what is happening in the relationship and why it hurts. The label just gives the person a name, at which point we likely stop asking questions.

You Don’t Need to Diagnose Someone to Take Their Behavior Seriously

Part of the appeal of these labels is that they provide validation. If someone has treated you badly, especially over a long period of time, finding a word that seems to explain everything can feel like a relief. Suddenly the confusing relationship makes sense. There are literally articles about it. There are videos describing exactly what you’ve experienced. And other people have stories that sound just like yours. I understand why that feels so powerful.

But you don’t need to prove that someone has a personality disorder before you’re allowed to be hurt by them. Your partner can be controlling without having NPD. Your parent can repeatedly dismiss your feelings without having NPD. Your friend can make everything about herself without having NPD. And your ex can lie, cheat, manipulate, behave selfishly, or treat you terribly without having NPD. You are still allowed to decide that the behavior isn’t acceptable. A diagnosis doesn’t make harmful behavior more harmful, and the absence of a diagnosis doesn’t make it OK.

Sometimes Labels Keep Us Stuck

There’s another downside to diagnosing people from afar. Once you’ve decided someone is a narcissist, you may start interpreting everything they do through that lens. An apology becomes manipulation, kindness becomes love-bombing, a disagreement becomes gaslighting, or withdrawing becomes the silent treatment. Maybe some of those interpretations are accurate. But if every possible behavior becomes evidence for the diagnosis you’ve already assigned, there’s no longer much room for curiosity or context. That’s not psychological insight. That’s confirmation bias with therapy language.

Sometimes the label becomes the focus when the relationship itself should be. The more useful question isn't whether your partner is a narcissist. It's whether you feel respected in the relationship you're actually in. Can you disagree without being punished for it? Can this person take responsibility when they've hurt you? Do your needs seem to matter as much as theirs? Can the two of you repair things after a fight instead of just moving past them? And, importantly, do you like who you are when you're with them? Those answers matter whether your partner meets criteria for any diagnosis at all.

Use Your Words

We teach children to “Use your words” when they’re overwhelmed because specificity helps us understand each other. Adults could use a little more of that, too. Instead of “She’s a narcissist,” tell me what she actually does. For example, she rarely asks about you, or becomes furious when you disagree with her. Maybe your partner needs to control how you spend money, can never seem to admit when he’s wrong, makes jokes at your expense and then tells you you’re too sensitive, or expects you to prioritize his needs without doing the same for you. Now we’re talking about something real.

We can look at patterns, talk about boundaries, decide what needs to change, and determine whether the relationship is workable. We can do all of that without diagnosing someone from the other side of the dinner table.

Mental health language can help us understand ourselves and each other. But when every difficult person becomes a narcissist, every disagreement becomes gaslighting, and every uncomfortable feeling becomes a trigger, the language stops helping.

Your ex may not be a narcissist. They may be selfish, controlling, emotionally unavailable, or sometimes just an *sshole. And that may be all the information you need to decide you don’t want to be with them anymore.

item.title: Why We Lie About Who We Are
item.description:
Fantasies

Why We Lie About Who We Are

From Cambridge dons to Victorian dancers, the same impulse keeps showing up.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Academics aren't the only ones prone to a touch of fabulism; we all are, just less dramatically.
  • Some people invent entire identities and keep the act going for decades without cracking.
  • The psychology behind extreme lying has very little to do with confidence.

Jason Arday has dominated the British news media this week. I cannot remember a story building this fast, breaking news of fresh tidbits in the ongoing saga of the Cambridge professor whose version of events has come under sustained and very public challenge. The reality is that academics have always been known to suffer from a touch of fabulism. As an academic myself, I can understand the temptation to big up your research a bit, if only to stand out in an overcrowded and highly competitive arena. Arday isn't the first or last person to over-inflate a CV, and the phenomenon has always intrigued me. Not in the way the right have glommed onto it, like manna from heaven: Look, see, DEI gone mad! I'm more intrigued by why someone would stretch the truth to that extent.

Why Do Fabulists Deceive?

Fabulists have always fascinated me. Usually, a sense of fear or shame stops us from spinning elaborate fairy stories to impress others, and we grow out of it in childhood. I recall telling everyone in my class as a child that I had not one, but two full-size Olympic swimming pools and a pony at home. But why do others carry the habit into adulthood? Are they not afraid of getting caught out? The thing with Arday is that some of the claims attributed to him were so easily checkable that you have to wonder whether he ever worried it would unravel.

I've always believed it's a particular skillset to utterly convince everyone you're something you're not, and it takes a level of dedication that astounds me. When the Hilaria Baldwin story broke years ago, instead of being disgusted by the long-held ruse, I was captivated. Hilaria famously pretended to be Spanish for more than a decade, when she's actually from Massachusetts, even going so far as to "mispronounce" the word cucumber on TV. "How do you say this," she asked her co-host, in a thick Spanish accent, "cucumber?" Look up the clip on YouTube if you're ever having imposter syndrome. But rather than being enraged at the audacity, I'm always fascinated. I wish I could ask Hilaria: But why? In typical researcher mode, I want to know what makes someone want to fake their entire identity, and the commitment it takes to stick to it. That's a Meryl Streep-level of commitment to the craft.

This story isn't anything new. Fakers and grifters have been around for years, except nowadays, with the dawn of the internet, it's easier to sniff out the con. I was flabbergasted, as an Irish person, to learn that the feted Irish playwright Micheál MacLiammóir, who wrote the brilliant Ill Met by Moonlight, wasn't Irish at all, despite having the most Irish-sounding name imaginable. There are plenty of fascinating historical examples. The famous Victorian-era "Spanish" dancer Lola Montez gained global fame and recognition, but turned out not to be Spanish at all. She was actually Irish. She was the Hilaria Baldwin of her day.

So what are the psychological motivations for pretending you're someone you're not?

Pseudologia Fantastica

The clinical term for extreme, sustained fabrication like this is pseudologia fantastica, sometimes called pathological lying or mythomania. It's not formally recognised in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition, which is part of why cases like this are so hard to pin down legally as well as psychologically, but a recent systematic review of documented cases found the most common motives were self-aggrandisement, attention-seeking, and what researchers call "sick-role assumption," essentially, the pull of being seen as exceptional or deserving of sympathy (Kainth et al., 2026), who identified self-aggrandisement in 38.2 percent of cases, attention-seeking in 36.4 percent, and sick-role assumption in 29.1 percent, with lies most often centred on health, occupational, or educational achievements. The same review found the fabrications clustered heavily around personality and mood disorders, and elevated rates of trauma history, suggesting that for at least some fabulists, the lie isn't calculated so much as compulsive, a way of managing an underlying wound rather than a cold strategic play.

There's a lighter, more universal cousin at work too. Leary and Kowalski's foundational impression management research argues that most of us manage the impressions we give off constantly, and that the motivation ramps up sharply when our audience is large, when the stakes for reward or rejection are high, and when there's a gap between how we currently look and how we wish we looked (Leary & Kowalski, 1990). Job interviews and first dates are the textbook examples. A hyper-competitive academic job market or a talk show green room is simply a higher-stakes version of the same pressure. Most of us just stop short of the swimming pools and the pony.

Which is maybe the most honest answer to my own question. The line between a fabulist and the rest of us isn't motivation; we all want to look good in front of an audience that matters to us. The line is where the impulse to embellish gets checked by shame, by fear of exposure, or simply by growing up. For a small number of people, that checking mechanism seems to fail, or was never quite built.
